content: Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT) is a condition characterized by abnormal glucose metabolism, which is often associated with insulin resistance. It represents a pre-diabetic state and is linked to an increased risk of developing cardiovascular diseases. IGT can precede the onset of type 2 diabetes mellitus by several years and is also considered a risk factor for increased mortality. The World Health Organization (WHO) and the American Diabetes Association (ADA) define impaired glucose tolerance as a two-hour plasma glucose level between 140 and 199 mg/dL (7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L) during a 75-gram oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). A diagnosis of IGT is made when a patient exhibits elevated glucose levels two hours after the glucose load, but these levels are not high enough to meet the diagnostic criteria for type 2 diabetes mellitus. Fasting glucose levels in individuals with IGT may be normal or only mildly elevated. It is estimated that approximately 10 to 15 percent of adults in the United States have either IGT or a related condition. Certain medications have been associated with the development of glucose intolerance. These include: Asparaginase derived from Erwinia chrysanthemi Estramustine Medroxyprogesterone acetate Megestrol Pegaspargase The progression from IGT to type 2 diabetes mellitus and the associated risk of cardiovascular disease is higher compared to individuals with impaired fasting glycemia. While pharmacological interventions can delay the onset of diabetes in some cases, lifestyle modifications are the cornerstone of prevention and management. Patients diagnosed with IGT are strongly encouraged to engage in regular physical activity and adopt a balanced diet that minimizes the intake of empty calories, particularly from sugar. Additionally, carnitine supplementation has been shown to temporarily enhance glucose uptake, regulation, and oxidation, but its effects are only sustained while carnitine levels remain elevated in the bloodstream.
